expect: Recovery from knee replacement is a gradual process, with most people walking with assistance early on and steadily gaining strength and motion over several months. Your surgeon will give you your own timeline.

items.text: Ask your therapist for a pre-surgery exercise plan
items.detail: Gentle leg strengthening before surgery may help short-term pain and function; benefits tend to fade by a few months, so treat it as a head start.

items.text: Practice getting up from a chair safely
items.detail: Standing and sitting with support, if your therapist recommends it, prepares you for early walking after surgery.
Therapists often begin on day 0 or 1; do the exercises you are taught several times a day.
Early therapy emphasizes safe walking with a walker or crutches, building confidence and balance as swelling decreases.

items.text: Strengthen legs and improve stair navigation
items.detail: Most patients work on climbing stairs and strengthening muscles to regain independence in daily activities.

items.text: Ask if you will need a knee brace
items.detail: Practice varies: some surgeons use a brace early on and many do not. Follow your surgeon's instructions.

items.text: Prepare an ice pack and a pillow for propping your leg
items.detail: Ice for about 20 minutes at a time can ease swelling and pain. Prop your calf or foot; avoid a pillow directly under the knee.

items.text: Set up a sturdy armchair or recliner at a safe height
items.detail: A high-back chair with armrests makes sitting and standing easier; add a cushion if your seating is too low.

items.text: Ask your surgeon about sleeping positions
items.detail: Many people can sleep in any position, but avoid a pillow or towel under the operated knee. Your surgeon may have specific advice.

items.text: Install grab bars in the bathroom
items.detail: Bars near the toilet and shower can help with balance during early recovery.

items.text: Bring any walker or crutches you were given
items.detail: If your team supplied a walking aid or brace before the hospital stay, bring it. Hospitals often supply aids on loan.
Many people are allowed full weight on the leg as pain allows, but some are not; follow your surgeon's specific instructions.
Avoid lifting heavy objects or bending deeply; your surgeon will tell you what movements to avoid and when to resume them.

items.text: Discuss return to work based on your job
items.detail: Office work is often possible around 6 weeks; physically demanding jobs may need several more weeks. Your surgeon will advise based on your progress.

items.text: Ask which surgical approach and implant type you will have
items.detail: The technique (such as minimally invasive or traditional) and implant design can affect recovery speed and restrictions; programs differ, so follow your surgeon’s plan.

items.text: Get a raised toilet seat or frame
items.detail: It makes getting on and off the toilet easier; a commode is an option if your only toilet is on another floor.

items.text: Ask about compression stockings and blood clot prevention
items.detail: Some surgeons advise stockings for several weeks and prescribe blood thinners; follow your team's instructions.
